name: Repository
intent: Give the domain code a collection-like object for loading and saving things, so it never touches the storage details.
scenario: An order service lists a customer's open orders and cancels one. It should not care whether orders live in memory, in SQL or behind a web API.
problem: The order service builds its own queries and reads rows. Every service that needs orders repeats the SQL, tests need a real database, and moving the data to another store means editing every service that touched it.
solution: Define an OrderRepository interface that speaks the language of the domain: add(order), get(id), findOpenFor(customer). The service depends only on that interface. One class per store implements it, and it alone knows the queries. Tests pass in an in-memory version. The repository behaves like a collection of orders, not like a database connection.
pain: OrderService builds SQL strings and reads raw rows
Four other services copy the same query with small differences
Unit tests need a running database
Changing the store means editing every service
benefits: Each query lives in one place and can be tuned there
Tests use a fast in-memory repository
A new store is one new class, with no service edited
whenToUse: Domain code should be testable without a database
The same lookups are needed by several services
Storage may change, or more than one store is used (cache, SQL, API)
whenNotToUse: A small script or CRUD screen where the ORM or query call is already clear enough
The ORM already offers a collection-like session and you would only wrap it one-to-one
Reports that join many tables: use a query service made for reading instead
pitfalls: Hiding cost: a collection-like call in a loop can run one query per item
A generic repository with every possible filter becomes a second query language
Leaking storage details, such as returning query builders or table rows, defeats the point
One repository per table, rather than per aggregate, spreads one rule over many classes

roles.label: Client
roles.description: Domain or application code that needs entities. It sees only the repository interface.

roles.label: Repository
roles.description: Interface with collection-like methods written in the language of the domain.

roles.label: Concrete repository
roles.description: One implementation per store: memory, SQL, a remote API. The only place that knows queries.

roles.label: Entity
roles.description: The domain object that is loaded and saved.

quiz.question: A team has OrderService calling a repository that is backed by SQL. A new requirement says orders older than a year must come from an archive service instead. Where should the change go?
options: Add a new branch to OrderService that asks the archive service when the order is old
Copy OrderService into an ArchivedOrderService and let callers pick the one they need
Put the archive call inside the repository, so callers still ask for an order by id
Change every caller to check the order date before it decides which store to ask
quiz.explanation: Where an order lives is a storage decision, which is what the repository hides. Keeping it there leaves OrderService and all other callers unchanged. The other options push storage rules into domain or caller code, so each caller must learn them.

quiz.question: A page shows 50 customers with their open orders. The code calls repository.findOpenFor(customer) in a loop and the page takes seconds, because it runs 50 queries. What is the best fix?
options: Remove the repository and let the page run its own SQL, since the interface causes the slowness
Add a batch method such as findOpenForAll(customers) that loads them in one query
Cache the result of every call for an hour so that repeat visits skip the queries
Make the loop run in parallel so that the 50 queries finish at about the same time
quiz.explanation: The loop is the cost, and a collection-like interface can hide it. A method shaped for the use case lets the repository answer in one query and still keep the storage details inside. Dropping the repository, caching or parallel calls leave the query count or the coupling in place.

quiz.question: A developer adds a generic repository with find(filter) that accepts any field, operator and sort order, so every future query can use it. A year later callers build long filter objects. What went wrong?
options: The repository should have returned raw rows so that callers could filter them themselves
Nothing, because a more flexible interface is always the better repository design in practice
The filter should have been written in SQL strings so that each caller is exact
The repository turned into a second query language, and its meaningful methods were lost
quiz.explanation: A repository is useful because its methods are named for what the domain asks, such as findOpenFor. A fully generic find moves the query building back to callers, and the storage shape leaks with it. Raw rows or SQL strings make that worse.
